This is following on from the thread: #general > Proving an open conjecture with AI + Lean

That thread is related to the N = 8 Thomson problem. In the meantime, the N = 7 case has also been proven in Lean here.

There is a natural question how far can we extend these methods, can we do e.g. the N = 9 case or beyond?

There is also the question of proving or disproving the conjecture at the bottom of this section on the Wikipedia page.

There is also the question of whether we want to do this?

cc @Mitchell Taylor
I think it is also a question still how formalizable the n=5 case is in Lean because it uses interval arithmetic heavily. I know someone is working on that. Does this method give a simpler n=5 proof?

I think formalizing the known cases in Lean would be super interesting, as they are computer assisted. For the unknown cases, there is certainly interest in extending the methods to other N. Certain N (like N=7) are quite easy given the techniques developed for N=8, but others are not. How about I talk to the members of the energy optimization community who have thought the most about these types of problems and get back to you with their opinions on how to proceed?
This sounds like the best strategy here. Thanks @Mitchell Taylor
How do the proofs for different N depend on each other?

A priori, they don't. Commonalities may include the three point bound, symmetry reductions and a computer-assisted proof, but whether one can execute this depends a lot on the structure of the proposed global minimizer.

Hi all, I've put together an AI-made Lean warrant for the 7-point case with the logarithmic energy (not the Coulomb version): https://github.com/alejandrozarco/thomson-n7-log
I haven't checked it myself, so I'm not claiming the problem is solved. There's an overview in the repo explaining how it fits together. Would anyone be willing to take a look?
Hi Alex, this would be easier to check if you use comparator
Hi Joseph, comparator is running, I'll report back here when it completes. The config used is lean/comparator.json

Comparator is done and passes, using the config in lean/comparator.json. It ran without the landrun sandbox. Details are in verification/lean/comparator_2026-10-02.txt. A second independent checker (nanoda) also accepted it.

so the lean looks ok, the statement Challenge.lean I can't say for sure, if anyone could check that it matches conjecture 1 of Armentano et al., that would be great.

Jason Rute said:

I think it is also a question still how formalizable the n=5 case is in Lean because it uses interval arithmetic heavily. I know someone is working on that. Does this method give a simpler n=5 proof?

On the n=5 case: I was developing https://github.com/archiebrowne/Thomson for a while until I ran out of tokens. The state of that project is just a single sorry left (though it seemed like a tough one). From what I can tell, all of the mathematical arguments are finalised, it's just the computational stuff that is left, and the statements of these results live in https://github.com/archiebrowne/Thomson/blob/main/Thomson/Computational.lean, whilst the challenge file is at https://github.com/archiebrowne/Thomson/blob/main/challenge.lean. If anyone wants to build on this then please feel free, I'd be interested in working together to try and get this finalised!
